title: I Saw the Future of Robotics in a Virtual Duck That Chases My Cat
gist: Will Knight reports that OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol and Astra models can now build robot simulations and run training loops in hours instead of weeks, using Nvidia's Isaac Sim/Newton, with Berkeley's Ken Goldberg and Nvidia's Jim Fan open-sourcing the Aspire agentic robot framework. Reliability remains hard, but industrial automation firms are interested and a 'vibe robotics' wave may follow.

insights.claim: Wired's Will Knight coded and trained a simulated Pollen Robotics/Hugging Face Microduck robot to walk and identify cats in a few hours using OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol, work he says previously would have taken weeks.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Order-of-magnitude cuts in robot-training labor lower the barrier to robotics development, widening the market for sim tools and hobbyist hardware.
insights.quote: I was able to code and train the virtual robot in just a few hours, which is, quite frankly, incredible.
insights.locator: I was able to code and train

insights.claim: OpenAI's latest models are strong at understanding and manipulating 3D representations of the physical world and translating that into code, agentic actions and robot training.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Spatial/3D competence is becoming a differentiator for frontier models, opening robotics as a new demand vertical for model providers.
insights.quote: remarkably good at understanding and manipulating 3D representations of the physical world

insights.claim: Given access to Nvidia's Newton tool and a video clip of a real robot, OpenAI's Astra produced a full 3D simulation with camera position, lighting, background and materials set within an hour, per UC Berkeley professor Ken Goldberg's lab.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Automating sim-scene construction removes a key bottleneck in sim-to-real robot training; watch Nvidia's simulation stack adoption.
insights.quote: within an hour it had produced a full 3D simulation with all the parameters set

insights.claim: Beyond writing code, GPT-6 Sol drove Nvidia Isaac Sim, watched videos of the virtual robot to assess performance, and suggested tweaks to its training regime, automating the experiment loop of robot training.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: LLMs closing the train-evaluate-adjust loop means robotics R&D scales with compute rather than scarce engineer time.
insights.locator: It used a piece of Nvidia software

themes.theme: Nvidia's role in the robot AI stack

insights.claim: The author's robot-training stack combined OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol, Nous Research's Hermes agentic harness, and an Nvidia DGX Spark personal AI computer, with Nvidia software (Isaac Sim, Newton) used for simulation.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Nvidia captures value at both the hardware (DGX Spark) and simulation-software layers even when the reasoning model comes from OpenAI.
insights.locator: This is precisely what I found

insights.claim: Nvidia researcher Jim Fan argues that LLMs now control robots the way software agents use computer applications, calling visual language action (VLA) models as tools.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: A tool-calling architecture lets general LLMs orchestrate specialized motor-control models, favoring modular robotics stacks.
insights.quote: LLMS can use models trained to control physical actions—visual language action (VLA) models—just as they access different software on a computer.
insights.locator: Jim Fan, a researcher at Nvidia

insights.claim: Jim Fan, Ken Goldberg and others open-sourced Aspire, an agentic robot framework that lets robots discover and use new skills; in one demo GPT-6 Astra learned to solve a Rubik's cube with two robot arms after long reasoning.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Open-source agentic robotics frameworks can commoditize skill acquisition and accelerate adoption across labs.
insights.quote: it eventually is able to solve it because it learns the skills over time
insights.locator: This week, Fan, Goldberg, and others

insights.claim: At the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, Jim Fan demoed Astra controlling a robot arm that painted the Golden Gate Bridge with nearby paint and brushes.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Research community sentiment at CoRL signals rapid convergence of frontier LLMs and robotics.
insights.locator: At the Conference on Robot Learning

insights.claim: Getting robots to work reliably and efficiently is still extremely difficult and requires significant engineering expertise; the author's Microduck vision system is not good enough for a real product, and a moonwalk attempt failed.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Expect a lag between demo-grade AI robotics and deployable products; temper near-term revenue expectations.
insights.locator: Of course, getting robots to work reliably

insights.claim: Ken Goldberg says a number of industrial robotics and automation firms have shown interest in AI-driven robot training, which could soon have an enormous impact on manufacturing and e-commerce.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Industrial automation vendors adopting LLM-driven training could compress deployment costs in warehouses and factories.
insights.locator: Still, the ease and speed of training

insights.claim: The author predicts a 'vibe robotics' wave analogous to vibe coding, as hobbyists and engineers realize how easy it has become to program and train robots.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Watch for hobbyist robot hardware (e.g., Hugging Face/Pollen) and sim tooling demand as a leading indicator.
insights.locator: Much like vibe coding a few years ago
